QF.id: AIFM CII Fund Performance and Benchmarking_23

question.text: Why are Sharpe ratio and Sortino ratio less directly applicable as headline performance metrics for Category I/II AIFs than for listed-equity portfolios?

answer.text: Sharpe and Sortino are SEBI-prohibited for Cat I/II AIFs.
Cat I/II AIFs invest in illiquid, unlisted securities without regular observable price series, making volatility (standard deviation) hard to compute meaningfully — IRR/TVPI/DPI are more apt.
Sharpe and Sortino require a negative risk-free rate.
Cat I/II AIFs always have zero beta, so the ratios are undefined.

explanation.text: The Logic: Sharpe = (Rp - Rf)/σp and Sortino uses downside deviation. Both require a time series of returns with defensible volatility estimates. Cat I/II portfolios have unlisted holdings with only periodic mark-to-model valuations, so σ is smoothed/stale — producing artificially flattering ratios. Chapter 7 emphasises cash-flow metrics (IRR, MOIC, TVPI, DPI, RVPI) and PME/Direct Alpha over Sharpe/Sortino. The Trap: SEBI does not prohibit them (A). Risk-free rate is positive (C). Beta is non-zero for Cat I/II — it is unobservable, not zero (D). Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B Portfolio Managers can meaningfully report Sharpe/Sortino because PMS holds listed securities with observable prices. Cat III AIFs (XIX-E/XIX-B) can use them more than Cat I/II because Cat III trades liquid/listed exposures. Manager's Pro-Tip: If a consultant LP insists on Sharpe for your Cat I/II fund, provide it but add a footnote: 'Volatility estimate based on quarterly fair-value marks — illiquidity smoothing understates risk.' This pre-empts methodology disputes.
